23.0.0.en: 1 The burden of Tyre. Howl, ye ships of Tarshish; for it is laid waste, so that there is no house, no entering in: from the land of Chittim it is revealed to them. 2 Be still, ye inhabitants of the isle; thou whom the merchants of Zidon, that pass over the sea, have replenished. 3 And by great waters the seed of Sihor, the harvest of the river, is her revenue; and she is a mart of nations. 4 Be thou ashamed, O Zidon: for the sea hath spoken, even the strength of the sea, saying, I travail not, nor bring forth children, neither do I nourish up young men, nor bring up virgins. 5 As at the report concerning Egypt, so shall they be sorely pained at the report of Tyre. 6 Pass ye over to Tarshish; howl, ye inhabitants of the isle. 7 Is this your joyous city, whose antiquity is of ancient days? her own feet shall carry her afar off to sojourn. 8 Who hath taken this counsel against Tyre, the crowning city, whose merchants are princes, whose traffickers are the honourable of the earth? 9 The LORD of hosts hath purposed it, to stain the pride of all glory, and to bring into contempt all the honourable of the earth. 10 Pass through thy land as a river, O daughter of Tarshish: there is no more strength. 11 He stretched out his hand over the sea, he shook the kingdoms: the LORD hath given a commandment against the merchant city, to destroy the strong holds thereof. 12 And he said, Thou shalt no more rejoice, O thou oppressed virgin, daughter of Zidon: arise, pass over to Chittim; there also shalt thou have no rest. 13 Behold the land of the Chaldeans; this people was not, till the Assyrian founded it for them that dwell in the wilderness: they set up the towers thereof, they raised up the palaces thereof; and he brought it to ruin. 14 Howl, ye ships of Tarshish: for your strength is laid waste.

23.0.1.en: We have already spoken about Tyre in our commentary on the Book of Ezekiel [Ezek 26].

23.0.2.en: The word “Tsor” (tsor) means “rock,” perhaps because the city was built on a rocky island. St. Jerome, however, holds that the word “Tyre” in Hebrew means “trial,” and so he sees its inhabitants as pointing to those who fall under the trial of Satan and his afflictions.

23.0.3.en: Keith and Urquhart hold that what is said in this chapter about Tyre was fulfilled literally.

23.0.4.en: Tyre fell under siege several times. Shalmaneser besieged it for five years and was not able to take it; Nebuchadnezzar besieged it for 13 years without success; Alexander the Great besieged it and took it after seven months in 332 B.C., and he destroyed it. Antigonus also besieged it, and in the Middle Ages it was besieged several times by the Crusaders. This Tyre is also counted responsible for the outbreak of the First World War, in which about 40 million people died, for it was kindled by Germany's attempt to build a railway between Berlin and Baghdad in order to develop trade with the countries of the Middle East.

23.0.5.en: What is stated here does not concern one particular siege of Tyre; rather, it represents what befalls every soul that imitates Tyre in being entangled with wealth and abominations.

23.0.6.en: The prophet describes the siege of Tyre, saying: “The burden of Tyre. Howl, ye ships of Tarshish; for it is laid waste, so that there is no house, no entering in: from the land of Chittim it is revealed to them” [1]. Here he brings out the effect of the destruction that befell Tyre upon the sailors of the merchant ships returning from Tarshish. It appears that they had not heard of the collapse of the city, and so they were astounded when they found no entrance to the city, for its walls had been torn down, and they found not a single house. The news, because of its gravity, spread until it reached Chittim, that is, the island of Cyprus, as a sign that all the nations of Europe heard of this event. Some hold that this siege was carried out by the Macedonian army, the army of Alexander the Great, coming from the island of Cyprus.

23.0.7.en: The prophet calls the neighboring cities to lament the state of Tyre, for she had been a source of good for them through trade, and now she has been utterly destroyed, and some cities lost a great deal of profit.

23.0.8.en: The merchants of Zidon heard (Zidon means “fishing”; it is about 22 miles north of Tyre and is considered the mother city of Tyre, so she came lamenting the state of her daughter). The merchants who used to go about in her streets came, and they were stunned at what had befallen her; they could not utter a word, but deep grief came upon them. As for the Egyptians, the dwellers of the Nile valley, they grieved because Tyre was an important center for the export of their produce and crops in exchange for the goods of Tyre. The prophet refers to the river Nile by the word “Sihor,” which means “disturbance” (Isa 22:3).

23.1.0.en: So Zidon grieves over her humbled, indeed collapsed, daughter “Tyre,” who had been like the bride of the Mediterranean Sea, or like a crowned queen who refreshed many lands in Africa and Europe. Now she has become like a spinster who groans in isolation, without husband or sons; she has lost the many lands that were like sons to her [4].

23.1.1.en: Egypt grieved because it lost an important center for exporting its produce, and perhaps because it feared that what befell Tyre would befall it. This is what happened in the days of Nebuchadnezzar, who plundered the wealth of Pharaoh after besieging Tyre (Ezek 29:17-20).

23.1.2.en: The prophet asks the remnant that remains in Tyre to depart to Tarshish, an ancient city in Spain and one of the flourishing colonies of Tyre. They departed wailing, because they were fleeing as refugees. Some hold that the prophet said this as a kind of mockery of the inhabitants of Tyre, who had been arrogant since ancient times: here they are, departing in terror and fear to live as strangers and refugees.

23.1.3.en: The prophet puts a theological question that stirs the hearers to search for the answer: “Who hath taken this counsel against Tyre, the crowning city, whose merchants are princes, whose traffickers are the honourable of the earth?” In other words, who has passed judgment on Tyre the crowned queen, who made of her colonies princes and rulers, and of her merchants honorable nobles throughout the whole world? She was a rich queen who poured out wealth, luxury and honor, together with pride, upon the nations that dealt with her. Who, then, has judged her thus?

23.2.0.en: The LORD of hosts is the One who purposed this [9], to bring her pride down to the dust and to bring into contempt all her merchants, men of dignity and worldly honor. This is what the prophet Amos meant when he said: “Shall there be evil in a city, and the LORD hath not done it?” (Amos 3:6). Father Theodoret says: [When divine judgment speaks to human beings, it speaks to them according to their language and their human feelings. The physician cuts or cauterizes those who suffer from sores for the sake of their health, and yet those who cannot bear it see that as an evil.]

23.2.1.en: God purposed this, but the cause of the ruin is pride and vainglory. It is sin that corrupts man as it does the nations, and God's judgment is only a declaration of what man brings upon himself by himself.

23.3.0.en: The prophet likens Tyre, fleeing after the destruction, to a woman who has lost everything and crosses the river Nile without a girdle to bind her garments; or he likens her to the waters of the Nile at its mouth, which pour into the sea with no one able to stop them. So the people of Tyre fled from their shattered city, without strength or power, as though the waters were sweeping them toward the sea [10]. Therefore he calls her “thou oppressed virgin, daughter of Zidon” [12].

23.4.0.en: The Lord stretched out His hand in wrath over the sea, that is, He commanded the kingdoms to rise up against Phoenicia (Canaan) to destroy her strongholds [11] and shatter her pride, so that she no longer rejoices [12]; and instead of being a queen she becomes a disgraced virgin, who flees to Chittim (Cyprus) and finds no rest... What does this mean?

23.4.1.en: A. The Lord stretched out His hand calling to repentance, but Tyre did not respond to the call, and so the hand was stretched out for punishment. The Lord of glory also spread out His hands on the cross in love; whoever believed found in the cross the power of God unto salvation, and whoever rejected it came under judgment.

23.4.2.en: B. Tyre was to flee to Chittim... but she found no rest, for man's peace does not depend on the place where he is but on the depths of his inner soul. Man's rest is not in changing his place or his work or his social circumstances, but in returning to God his Savior, who calls: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Mt 11:28). As St. John Saba says: [Blessed is he who seeks You within him every hour; from Him life flows to him that he may delight in it.]

23.4.3.en: Since God knew that Tyre would not listen to this voice, He asked her to take warning from what happened to the Chaldeans at the hand of the king of Assyria, for he turned their palaces into a ruin.

23.5.0.en: 15 And it shall come to pass in that day, that Tyre shall be forgotten seventy years, according to the days of one king: after the end of seventy years shall Tyre sing as an harlot. 16 Take an harp, go about the city, thou harlot that hast been forgotten; make sweet melody, sing many songs, that thou mayest be remembered. 17 And it shall come to pass after the end of seventy years, that the LORD will visit Tyre, and she shall turn to her hire, and shall commit fornication with all the kingdoms of the world upon the face of the earth. 18 And her merchandise and her hire shall be holiness to the LORD: it shall not be treasured nor laid up; for her merchandise shall be for them that dwell before the LORD, to eat sufficiently, and for durable clothing.

23.5.1.en: In His love for mankind, God does not leave man in his corruption but offers him every possibility of salvation. Therefore, after the prophet portrayed the extent of the ruin that befell Tyre, he returned to speak of her renewal by the Lord the Savior.

23.6.0.en: She is left enslaved to Babylon for 70 years, which corresponds to the seventy years that the prophet Jeremiah foretold concerning the Babylonian captivity of Israel (Jer 29:10), as though the Gentiles share with Israel in this humiliation, because He has shut up all together in disobedience (Rom 11:32), that all may enjoy the Savior and mercy may be shown to all. Jerusalem was accused of being a harlot (Isa 1:21), and here Tyre bears the same accusation [16].

23.6.1.en: The period from the first year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar until Cyrus is exactly 70 years, during which the nations served Babylon.

23.7.0.en: The prophet describes Tyre as a harlot who sings in the public places to draw men to herself. So Tyre acted with her trade, which was bound up with corruption. But after she had gone about the world as though it were one city through which the harlot goes about, she fell under the dominion of Babylon for 70 years, in a humiliation in which she could not carry on her trade or spread corruption among the other nations, until she became forgotten. The world forgot her, but God will not forget her; rather, He turns her humiliation into glory. After her trade had been bound up with corruption, it returns to be bound up with the holy life in the Lord; her merchants become witnesses to the Gospel of salvation, as she enters with the Gentiles into the faith, to live the evangelical life and preach it. After she was in hunger and nakedness, not during the Babylonian captivity but during the bondage of sin, she has come into the presence of the Lord, eating of the bread of life so that she does not hunger, and enjoying the garment of Baptism so that she is not naked, as the Apostle says: “For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal 3:27). This is what the prophet meant by saying: “And her merchandise and her hire shall be holiness to the LORD: it shall not be treasured nor laid up; for her merchandise shall be for them that dwell before the LORD, to eat sufficiently, and for durable clothing” [18].

24.0.0.en: 1 Behold, the LORD maketh the earth empty, and maketh it waste, and turneth it upside down, and scattereth abroad the inhabitants thereof. 2 And it shall be, as with the people, so with the priest; as with the servant, so with his master; as with the maid, so with her mistress; as with the buyer, so with the seller; as with the lender, so with the borrower; as with the taker of usury, so with the giver of usury to him. 3 The land shall be utterly emptied, and utterly spoiled: for the LORD hath spoken this word. 4 The earth mourneth and fadeth away, the world languisheth and fadeth away, the haughty people of the earth do languish. 5 The earth also is defiled under the inhabitants thereof; because they have transgressed the laws, changed the ordinance, broken the everlasting covenant. 6 Therefore hath the curse devoured the earth, and they that dwell therein are desolate: therefore the inhabitants of the earth are burned, and few men left. 7 The new wine mourneth, the vine languisheth, all the merryhearted do sigh. 8 The mirth of tabrets ceaseth, the noise of them that rejoice endeth, the joy of the harp ceaseth. 9 They shall not drink wine with a song; strong drink shall be bitter to them that drink it. 10 The city of confusion is broken down: every house is shut up, that no man may come in. 11 There is a crying for wine in the streets; all joy is darkened, the mirth of the land is gone. 12 In the city is left desolation, and the gate is smitten with destruction. 13 When thus it shall be in the midst of the land among the people, there shall be as the shaking of an olive tree, and as the gleaning grapes when the vintage is done.

24.0.1.en: The prophet likens the whole earth to a vessel everything inside which has spoiled, so its owner empties it completely by turning it upside down. He says: “Behold, the LORD maketh the earth empty, and maketh it waste, and turneth it upside down, and scattereth abroad the inhabitants thereof. And it shall be, as with the people, so with the priest; as with the servant, so with his master; as with the maid, so with her mistress; as with the buyer, so with the seller; as with the lender, so with the borrower; as with the taker of usury, so with the giver of usury to him” [1-2].

24.0.2.en: Thus all were shut up in disobedience, all deserved death, and all needed a Savior able to renew their nature. The priest shares in this with the people, the great with the despised, the rich with the poor. This matter calls, as it were, for the emptying of the earth so that it returns to what it was before the creation of the world, void and empty, and the Lord Himself recreates it.

24.0.3.en: This is the theological foundation of salvation: that creation had become utterly corrupt and needed its Maker to renew its creation. As Pope Athanasius the Apostolic says: [This is like the portrait of a man painted on a panel, which then happens to be disfigured by external stains; it becomes necessary for the one whose portrait it is to come again to renew the image of the face on the same wood (the panel).]

24.0.4.en: What have sin and disobedience done to mankind? Mankind drew near to the fires of the divine wrath and was burned. The secret of the burning is man's disobedient will, which drags him toward destruction.

24.1.0.en: The prophet Isaiah offers a comparison that reveals the wretched state to which mankind has come. In the season of the vintage, people used to hold joyful celebrations: they would drink wine, sing with gladness, and make offerings to the poor. But when the time of gathering came, the vineyards proclaimed their mourning, for they bore no grapes; the players of tambourines stopped beating them; there was no one to sing and no one to rejoice, for every pleasure had fled from the face of the earth, and ruin came by the fire of God's wrath, so that everything in the world became ashes [7-12]. Thus he likens the world to a burned city turned to ashes, and to mournful, dry fields that bear no fruit. He likens it to an olive tree that has shed its leaves and become bare, with neither fruit nor leaves [13], and to a vine from which all its clusters have been taken away.

24.1.1.en: It is fitting for the priest to realize his need of salvation just like the people [2], and as St. Gregory of Nazianzus says: [In truth there is no distinction between the people and the priests...]

24.2.s.en: 2. The joy of the believers in the Lord:

24.2.0.en: 14 They shall lift up their voice, they shall sing for the majesty of the LORD, they shall cry aloud from the sea. 15 Wherefore glorify ye the LORD in the east, even the name of the LORD God of Israel in the isles of the sea. 16 From the uttermost part of the earth have we heard songs, even glory to the righteous. But I said, My leanness, my leanness, woe unto me! the treacherous dealers have dealt treacherously; yea, the treacherous dealers have dealt very treacherously.

24.2.1.en: In the midst of this ruin, which deprived mankind of its inner peace and joy, there is a holy remnant that proclaims its gladness and joy in the Lord through praise and psalmody.

24.2.2.en: “They shall lift up their voice, they shall sing for the majesty of the LORD, they shall cry aloud from the sea.

24.2.3.en: Wherefore glorify ye the LORD in the east, even the name of the LORD God of Israel in the isles of the sea.

24.2.4.en: From the uttermost part of the earth have we heard songs, even glory to the righteous” [14-16].

24.2.5.en: Here he speaks of the small remnant in the world that accepted the faith and returned to God. These live in the east, that is, they enjoy the Sun of Righteousness shining upon them (Mal 4:3). And lest anyone think that the east here is merely a place, he said: “in the isles of the sea glorify the name of the LORD,” to affirm that those who dwell in the west (the islands of the Mediterranean, west of Jerusalem) enjoy salvation together with those in the east.

24.2.6.en: The theme of the praise is “Glory to (Christ) the Righteous!”

24.3.0.en: 17 Fear, and the pit, and the snare, are upon thee, O inhabitant of the earth. 18 And it shall come to pass, that he who fleeth from the noise of the fear shall fall into the pit; and he that cometh up out of the midst of the pit shall be taken in the snare: for the windows from on high are open, and the foundations of the earth do shake. 19 The earth is utterly broken down, the earth is clean dissolved, the earth is moved exceedingly. 20 The earth shall reel to and fro like a drunkard, and shall be removed like a cottage; and the transgression thereof shall be heavy upon it; and it shall fall, and not rise again. 21 And it shall come to pass in that day, that the LORD shall punish the host of the high ones that are on high, and the kings of the earth upon the earth. 22 And they shall be gathered together, as prisoners are gathered in the pit, and shall be shut up in the prison, and after many days shall they be visited. 23 Then the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed, when the LORD of hosts shall reign in mount Zion, and in Jerusalem, and before his ancients gloriously.

24.3.1.en: The salvation that God offers to mankind kindles the hearts of the believers with joy and exultation, and it stirs up terror in the unbelieving deniers and also in the demons.

24.3.2.en: The enemy of good realized that a plundering had been carried out against him, for the cross drew many of the souls that the enemy had enslaved, and the Resurrection shattered all the powers of darkness and opened the gates of Paradise.

24.3.3.en: The prophet sees the enemy of good as a wild beast that fell into the nets, into a pit, and opened its mouth lamenting its state in despair, with fear and trembling [16-18]. He was terrified when he saw himself descending toward the abyss as into an exceedingly deep pit, while heaven and earth stood witnessing to the cross: “The windows from on high are open, and the foundations of the earth do shake; the earth is utterly broken down, the earth is clean dissolved, the earth is moved exceedingly” [18-19]; “In that day the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed, when the LORD of hosts shall reign in mount Zion and in Jerusalem” [23].

24.3.4.en: Thus nature bears witness to the weight of the sin that the Lord Christ bore for us, as though it were an exceedingly heavy mass thrust down upon the earth, splitting it and shaking it and stirring up earthquakes in it, until the moon was ashamed and the sun confounded at what sin had done. And on the other hand, nature stood, as it were, in shame and humiliation before what man did to his Savior and Redeemer.

24.4.0.en: By the cross we entered into the spiritual reign (Rev 20), where the LORD of hosts reigns in mount Zion in Jerusalem [23]; He reigns by the cross over the hearts of the believers, binding the devil and all his spiritual hosts as captives until the time of the apostasy comes [22], for He made a public show of them (Col 2:15), granting us authority to tread on serpents and scorpions and all the power of the enemy.

24.4.1.en: The sight of the cross shattered the enemy, declaring the divine glory before the elders [23], for the Apostles beheld the power of salvation and understood it in their lives as in their preaching.
